newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N calls for urgent study of HQ security flaws.
newsitem.headline: U.N calls for urgent study of HQ security flaws.

text.p: A panel of experts should be set up immediately to study security deficiencies at U.N. headquarters, especially in view of recent worldwide terrorist attacks, a U.N. watchdog panel said on Monday.

This was one of the recommendations in a report by the U.N. office of internal oversight services on a botched $1.5 million electronic security system installed at the entrances to the U.N. complex but never activated.

The report called for feasibility studies before undertaking any future projects involving new technology or where no in-house expertise is available. It also said a responsible experienced manager should be assigned to each project and a chain of command established and adhered to.

But it said responsibility for the financial loss resulting from the security system, involving computerized electronic identity cards and turnstiles, "could not be attributed to the acts of any particular staff member either individually or collectively."

A contract for the system was signed in March 1992. It was completed, tested and accepted by the United Nations in May 1993 but its activation was delayed for more than a year. In September 1994 it was annnounced the system would not be put into operation.

Among the report's recommendations was that the United Nations "should immediately establish a security working group made up of security professionals from various government agencies to evaluate current physical security and procedural policies with a view to identifying the deficiencies and needs of the organisation."
"This is an especially important issue, considering the recent wave of terrorist attacks worldwide and the vulnerability of the United Nations headquarters facilities," the report said.

It found that the project was not properly planned and that no one in the United Nations had any experience with the technology. Although a consultant was hired, his experience was "in building services and not in access control."
"The single most serious failure in the process was the absence of a strong management presence. There was no clear management over the life of the contract," the report said.

The justifications given for not activating the system were problems that U.N. upper management "should have reasonably expected when introducing not only a new technology but also a new operating procedure," it said.
